segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, let us too lay aside every weight and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set before us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: keeping our eyes fixed on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured a cross, disregarding its shame, and has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Consider him who has endured such opposition from sinners against themselves, so that you may not grow weary in your souls and lose heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You have not yet resisted to the point of blood in your struggle against sin,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, nor lose heart when you are corrected by him;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: for the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and flogs every son he accepts.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is for discipline that you are enduring. God is treating you as sons; for what son is there whom a father does not discipline?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you are without the discipline in which all have come to share, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Besides, we had the fathers of our flesh to discipline us, and we respected them. Shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For they disciplined us for a few days as seemed good to them, but he does so for our benefit, so that we may share in his holiness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All discipline seems for the moment to be a matter not of joy but of grief; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore straighten the slack hands and the weakened knees,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pursue peace with everyone, and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: watching that no one falls short of the grace of God, that no root of bitterness sprouts up and causes trouble, and through it many are defiled,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that no one is sexually immoral or profane like Esau, who for a single meal sold his own rights as firstborn.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you know that afterward too, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no room for turning back, though he sought it with tears.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you have not come to what can be touched, to blazing fire and darkness and gloom and storm,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the blast of a trumpet and a voice speaking words, a voice whose hearers begged that no further word be spoken to them;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they could not bear the command:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And so fearsome was the sight that Moses said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am full of fear and trembling.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, to a festal gathering

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in the heavens, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks something better than Abel.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: See that you do not refuse the one who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused the one who warned them on earth, much less shall we escape if we turn away from the one who warns from the heavens.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His voice shook the earth then, but now he has promised:

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heaven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now this “Yet once more” points to the removal of the things that are shaken, as things that have been made, so that the things that are not shaken may remain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be thankful, and through this let us worship God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and awe,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for indeed our God is a consuming fire.

notes.note: The Greek word covers a leader who goes first, a founder, and an originator. 'Pioneer' fits the picture of a race in which Jesus has already run the course ahead of the runners. 'Author' or 'founder', the older renderings, take the word as 'originator' and are equally defensible.

The Greek has no 'our'. Most translations supply it, making Jesus the one who begins and completes the believer's faith. Without it, the phrase can also present Jesus as the one who himself ran the course of faith from start to finish, the climax of the list of the faithful in chapter 11. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

notes.phrase: for the joy set before him
notes.traditional: for the joy that was set before him
notes.note: The preposition can mean 'for the sake of' or 'instead of'. On the first reading, which most interpreters follow, the joy is the reward ahead that made the cross worth enduring. On the second, Jesus chose the cross in place of a joy that was his for the taking. 'For' is used because verse 16 uses the same preposition for an exchange with a view to gain.

The Greek text translated here has the plural, 'against themselves', which is found in several of the earliest manuscripts. Other manuscripts have the singular, 'against himself', and most English versions follow them. The plural would mean that the sinners' opposition to Jesus was to their own harm, and it may echo the Septuagint's description of Korah's company in Numbers 16.

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for whipping, and it is the word the Septuagint uses in Proverbs 3:12, which is quoted here. The Hebrew of that verse reads differently ('as a father the son in whom he delights'). 'Chastises' softens a word that a first-century reader would have heard as physical punishment, used here as a picture of painful correction.

notes.phrase: It is for discipline that you are enduring
notes.note: The verb form can be a statement ('you are enduring') or a command ('endure'). Many translations take it as a command. The statement fits the explanation that follows, in which the author interprets what the readers are already going through.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice' translate the same Greek words. Here the word refers to a life of doing what is right, the harvest that discipline produces.

The verb normally means 'turn aside', which would give 'so that the lame may not stray from the path'. In medical writers it can describe a limb being dislocated, and the contrast with 'be healed' favours that sense here. Either reading is possible.

The traditional rendering is 'repentance', which most translations keep and which readers generally take to include a change of life. The Greek word denotes a change of course rather than a feeling of sorrow, and 'turning back' reflects that. It is disputed whether the author means that Esau found no way to repent, or that he found no way to get the decision reversed (see Genesis 27:30–40). 'No room for turning back' allows both.

'It' may refer to the blessing or to the turning back; both nouns are feminine in Greek and the pronoun fits either. In Genesis 27 Esau weeps and begs for the blessing, which favours the first. The second is closer in the sentence.

notes.traditional: the mount that might be touched
notes.note: Many manuscripts add 'mountain' here, probably drawn from verse 22, and many translations include it. The earliest witnesses lack it, and the text translated here follows them. The scene is Mount Sinai at the giving of the law (Exodus 19; Deuteronomy 4). The words could also be construed as 'a fire that can be touched and is burning'.

notes.traditional: to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly
notes.note: The word means a festival crowd, and it can attach to what precedes ('myriads of angels in festal gathering') or to what follows ('a festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn'). The punctuation of the Greek edition translated here joins it to what follows. Many translations take it with the angels.

The traditional rendering is 'church', which is near-universal. A first-century reader knew this word as the term for a civic assembly and as the Septuagint's word for Israel gathered before God, as at Sinai, the scene just described. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' keeps the picture of a people gathered.

The Greek phrase is literally 'let us have grace', and older translations render it so, meaning 'let us hold on to God's grace'. But 'to have grace' was a common idiom for 'to be grateful', and most modern translations take it that way here.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Hebrews, where 'covenant', 'testament' and 'will' compete (notably Hebrews 9:16–17 and Galatians 3:15), and readers need to see that it is one word.
A key term in Hebrews and John (with τελειωτής, τέλειος) where 'perfect', 'complete' and 'bring to its goal' are all defensible and variation would hide the thread.
Translated variously as 'patience', 'perseverance', 'endurance' and 'steadfastness' across Paul, James, Hebrews and Revelation; the verb ὑπομένω should match.
Translations alternate between 'serve' and 'worship' for this word of cultic service, and it needs to be kept distinct from προσκυνέω and δουλεύω across the New Testament.
The word-family (παιδεύω, παιδευτής) spans 'discipline', 'training', 'instruction' and 'punishment' in Hebrews, Paul, Luke and Revelation, and needs a consistent policy.
